summary: Describes how RFCs are published. The definitive version moved from plain text to XML using RFCXML, and different publication versions are rendered from it. It obsoletes RFC 7990 and updates the status of earlier documents.

eli5.summary: RFCs are now written in a structured source form, and the versions you read are made from it. This explains the steps. It replaces RFC 7990.

questions: what formats are rfcs published in
can an rfc be changed after publication
what is the definitive version of an rfc
subtitle: How RFCs are published: one definitive XML file, with HTML, text and PDF versions rendered from it.

tldr.problem: RFC 7990 assumed a single XML file per RFC and used the word canonical for two different things. Experience showed that an RFC's XML sometimes has to be corrected after publication.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9720 defines a definitive format (RFCXML), a definitive version, publication formats (HTML, plain text, PDF) and publication versions. It lets the RFC Production Center reissue either kind of version as long as the semantic content is preserved.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 7990 and changes the stability policy in RFC 9280 so that published RFCs may be reissued. It is itself updated by RFC 9920.

today: RFC 9720 is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 7990 and updates RFC 9280. It is itself updated by RFC 9920.

sections.title: Why the Format Rules Changed
sections.content:
RFC 7990 set up a new way of publishing RFCs, with a canonical format that carries everything needed to render the document in many forms. The first RFC published under that plan was RFC 8651 in October 2019, and all RFCs since have followed it.

This document is about producing the published RFC. It does not change how each stream develops and reviews Internet-Drafts. The RFC says the details are expected to keep changing as the community and the RFC Production Center (RPC) gain experience, and implementors are advised not to assume all changes will be backwards compatible.
sections.eli5: The way RFCs are made was changed once already. This note records what that change turned out to mean in practice and what the rules are now.

sections.title: Four New Terms
sections.content:
RFC 7990 used the term canonical format for two very different things. RFC 9720 replaces it with four terms:

  • Definitive format: RFCXML.
  • Definitive version: a published RFC in the definitive format.
  • Publication format: currently one of HTML, plain text and PDF.
  • Publication version: a published RFC in one of the publication formats.

It also renames xml2rfc version 3 to RFCXML, and renames the publishing body from RFC Editor to RFC Production Center (RPC).
sections.eli5: Instead of one fuzzy word, there are now clear names: the master copy and the copies you actually read.

sections.title: The Definitive Version
sections.content:
The definitive version is the final RFCXML file made by the RPC. It holds all the information intended for the RFC, so any question about what was intended is answered from this file. RFC 7991 is the original complete description of RFCXML.

The file is self-contained: features that reference external input are expanded, and it has no src attributes on <artwork> or <sourcecode> elements and no comments or processing instructions. It may contain SVG line art (RFC 7996), which also appears in the HTML version, and non-ASCII characters (RFC 7997), which appear in all publication versions.

The RPC may change the definitive version over time, but such changes must preserve the semantics of the original RFC. Reasons include RFCXML schema updates, errors found in the XML and changes to the tooling that produces the publication versions. The RPC keeps a public record of each reissue with a short reason.
sections.eli5: The master copy has everything in it, nothing left to look up elsewhere. It can be fixed if it has typos or the printing machines change, but the meaning must stay the same.

sections.title: Publication Versions and Archives
sections.content:
The RPC is permitted but not required to reissue publication versions. When deciding, it weighs the risk of semantic change against the consistency of the Series. When the XML changes, publication versions may change even if no difference is visible, and they may be regenerated when production tools change.

The RPC keeps an archived set of all definitive versions and of previously published publication versions. These must be available by the same access methods as current ones, and every archived set records the date the version was created or reissued. The RFC does not say how archives are stored or located; the RPC decides that in consultation with the technical community.
sections.eli5: The printed cards can be reprinted when needed, and the old ones are kept in a drawer with the date on them so anyone can look back.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 9280
sections.content:
Section 7.6 of RFC 9280 said Once published, RFC Series documents are not changed. RFC 9720 replaces that sentence with: Once published, RFCs may be reissued, but the semantic content of publication versions shall be preserved to the greatest extent possible.

It also adds a new section 7.8, Consistency, saying that RFCs are copyedited, formatted and then published, and may be reissued to maintain a consistent presentation. The RFC adds that updates to RFCXML applied to existing RFCs should preserve semantics, but that avoiding all risk is not required; understanding and limiting the risk is.
sections.eli5: The old rule was never to touch a published RFC. The new rule is that it can be reissued, as long as what it says stays the same.

sections.title: Risks of Reissuing
sections.content: Allowing changes introduces risk. An editing error could change a definitive or publication version unintentionally, and regenerating a publication version from the definitive one could do the same. That could corrupt a standard, practice or critical piece of protocol information and harm the reputation of the RFC Series. The RPC is expected to identify, track and actively mitigate these risks. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Fixing a printed card could accidentally introduce a mistake, so the people doing it must be careful and keep track.
